questions.question: The drag bucket of a candidate airfoil lies below the cruise Cl. Which change to the airfoil moves the bucket to a higher Cl, and what does it cost?
options: More camber, at the cost of more nose-down Cm and trim drag
Less camber, at the cost of a lower Clmax at the stall
More thickness, at the cost of a higher Cdmin in cruise
Less thickness, at the cost of a shallower spar and a heavier wing
questions.explanation: More camber moves the drag bucket to a higher Cl and raises Clmax. It costs more nose-down Cm and the trim drag that goes with it.

questions.question: A team has airfoil data measured at a Reynolds number lower than the one its wing has at the stall. If it uses the data as measured, what is the error in the stall estimate?
options: Clmax and αstall are both underestimated
Clmax and αstall are both overestimated
Clα is underestimated over the linear range
Only Cdmin is in error; the stall is unchanged
questions.explanation: A higher Reynolds number raises Clmax and αstall and lowers Cdmin, while Clα does not change. Data taken at a lower Reynolds number put the stall too early and Clmax too low.

questions.question: An invented conventional airfoil has t/c = 0.10 and flies at Cl = 0.4. With κ = 0.87 for a conventional airfoil and 0.95 for a supercritical one, what Mdd does the Korn relation give?
questions.explanation: Mdd = κ − t/c − 0.1 Cl = 0.87 − 0.10 − 0.04 = 0.73. The lift coefficient enters with a factor of 0.1, and 0.95 applies only to a supercritical airfoil.

questions.question: The comparison table scores the thickness ratio with the highest value as best. What does the thicker airfoil give the aircraft?
options: A deeper spar, so a lighter wing, and more fuel volume
A higher Mdd at the design Cl, so a faster cruise speed
A lower Cdmin, so less drag at the cruise and climb Cl
Less nose-down Cm, so less trim drag and tail load
questions.explanation: The criterion t/c traces to spar depth and fuel volume, and a deeper spar makes a lighter wing. The costs of thickness, a higher Cdmin and a lower Mdd, are scored on their own rows.

questions.question: The horizontal tail is given an aspect ratio below the wing's. What is the reason?
options: A low AR has a higher αstall, so the tail stalls after the wing
A low AR has a steeper CLα, so the tail can be smaller
A low AR has less induced drag, so the trim drag is lower
A low AR has a lower αstall, so the tail warns of the wing stall
questions.explanation: A low aspect ratio gives a shallow CLα and a high αstall. The tail then stalls after the wing, at the price of more induced drag.

questions.section: The pitch-up boundary of swept wings
questions.question: A swept wing plots in Region II of the pitch-up boundary, where the nose rises at stall. Which change moves it toward Region I?
options: A lower aspect ratio
A higher aspect ratio
A higher taper ratio λ
More quarter-chord sweep
questions.explanation: Region I lies below the limiting aspect ratio, so a lower AR moves the wing toward it. More sweep or a higher λ lowers the limit and leaves the wing deeper in Region II.

questions.question: A wing with a taper ratio of 0.3 is tip loaded, and it gets a large washout. What is the washout for?
options: To make the stall start inboard, so the ailerons stay effective
To make the stall start at the tip, so the nose drops at stall
To raise the wing lift at a given α, so the stall speed falls
To delay the stall at the root, where a tapered wing stalls first
questions.explanation: A tip-loaded wing reaches the airfoil Clmax outboard first. Washout lowers the incidence of the tip so the stall starts inboard, and it costs lift at a given α.

questions.section: Maximum lift of the clean wing
questions.question: An invented clean wing has Λc/4 = 45° (cos 45° = 0.707) and an airfoil with Clmax = 1.50 at the MGC and the stall Reynolds number. With the rapid estimate for CLmax0 and the sweep factor KΛ, what is the wing CLmax?
questions.explanation: CLmax0 = 0.9 × 1.50 = 1.35, and the sweep factor KΛ = cos Λc/4 gives 1.35 × 0.707 = 0.95. Stopping at 1.35 leaves out the sweep.
